questions.question: What two conditions must a list of vectors satisfy to be an eigenbasis?
options: It must span only the kernel of the operator.
It must be linearly dependent and contain one eigenvector.
It must contain every eigenvalue, and every vector must be zero.
It must be a basis, and every vector in the list must be an eigenvector.

questions.question: What does the matrix of an operator look like when written in an eigenbasis?
options: The zero matrix in every case
A matrix with all entries equal
Diagonal
Row echelon but not diagonal

questions.question: Why is the standard basis an eigenbasis for a diagonal matrix?
options: The standard basis is never made of eigenvectors.
The standard basis vectors are all zero vectors.
Each standard basis vector is scaled by one diagonal entry.
A diagonal matrix sends every vector to the same vector.

questions.question: How does an eigenbasis relate to diagonalizability?
options: An eigenbasis exists exactly when the matrix is singular.
An eigenbasis prevents diagonalization.
A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when an eigenbasis exists.
Every matrix has an eigenbasis over every field.

questions.question: Why must the vectors in an eigenbasis be independent?
options: Because every basis is linearly independent.
Because the zero vector is part of every basis.
Because every eigenvector is automatically independent of all others.
Because independence is needed only for rows, not vectors.

questions.question: For $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, which list is an eigenbasis of $ℝ^2$?
If $v_1$ and $v_2$ are independent eigenvectors in $ℝ^2$, what do they form?
options: Only a kernel basis
A row echelon matrix
A dependent list
An eigenbasis of $ℝ^2$

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has three independent eigenvectors. What exists?
options: An eigenbasis
A zero characteristic polynomial
No diagonalization
Only one eigendirection

questions.question: Why is the list $((1,0),(2,0))$ not an eigenbasis of $ℝ^2$, even if both vectors are eigenvectors?
options: There are too many vectors.
Eigenvectors cannot lie on coordinate axes.
The first vector is zero.
The vectors are linearly dependent, so not a basis

questions.question: If $P$ in a diagonalization has columns $v_1,v_2,v_3$, what must these columns form?
options: A row vector
A basis of the kernel only
A list of diagonal entries
An eigenbasis

questions.question: Can a list of eigenvectors fail to be an eigenbasis?
options: Yes, but only if the eigenvalues are real.
No, any eigenvector list is automatically an eigenbasis.
Yes, if it is not a basis of the whole space.
No, unless the determinant is zero.

questions.question: Why does an eigenbasis make the matrix diagonal rather than merely triangular?
options: The basis vectors are required to be orthogonal.
Eigenvectors always have only one nonzero coordinate.
Each basis vector goes to a scalar multiple of itself, unmixed
Triangular matrices have no eigenvectors.

questions.question: What information is placed on the diagonal once an operator is written in an eigenbasis?
options: The entries of the original first row.
The eigenvalues for the basis eigenvectors
The algebraic multiplicities only
The lengths of the basis vectors

questions.question: Let $Av_1=2v_1$, $Av_2=-v_2$, and $v_1,v_2$ be a basis of $ℝ^2$. What is the matrix of $A$ in this basis?
options: $\operatorname{diag}(-1,2)$
$\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: A $4$-dimensional space has only three independent eigenvectors for an operator. Can those vectors form an eigenbasis?
options: No, an eigenbasis would need four independent vectors.
No, because eigenbases are not allowed in dimension four.
Yes, if one eigenvalue is repeated.
Yes, three eigenvectors always form a basis.

questions.question: If the standard basis is an eigenbasis for $A$ with eigenvalues $5$ and $7$, what is $A$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\7&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\operatorname{diag}(7,5)$ necessarily
$\operatorname{diag}(5,7)$

questions.question: Why does the existence of an eigenbasis rule out defectiveness?
options: A defective matrix lacks enough eigenvectors for an eigenbasis
Because eigenbases contain the zero vector.
Because defective matrices have no eigenvalues.
Because defectiveness is about determinant only.

questions.question: If two eigenvectors correspond to the same eigenvalue, can they both appear in an eigenbasis?
options: No, repeated eigenvalues cannot occur in diagonalizable matrices.
No, an eigenbasis may contain at most one vector per eigenvalue.
Yes, even if they are scalar multiples.
Yes, provided they are linearly independent and help form a basis.

questions.question: In $ℝ^3$, suppose $v_1,v_2$ are independent eigenvectors for $λ=1$ and $v_3$ is an eigenvector for $λ=4$, with $v_1,v_2,v_3$ independent. What diagonal matrix is obtained in this eigenbasis order?
options: $\operatorname{diag}(4,1,1)$
$\operatorname{diag}(1,4,1)$
$\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4)$
$\operatorname{diag}(1,4,4)$

questions.question: An operator on $ℝ^2$ has eigenvectors $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ with eigenvalues $2$ and $3$, respectively. Do these vectors form an eigenbasis?
options: No, because they are not orthogonal.
No, because their eigenvalues are different.
Yes, because every pair of nonzero vectors is independent.
Yes, because the two eigenvectors are independent in $ℝ^2$.
